avLead: From Bhamb to the world — and back again. The people, places, and choices behind Uttara Farm.
av1p1: Vijay’s family traces eight generations back to Uttur, a village near Hyderabad in Andhra Pradesh. Ancestors migrated into Maharashtra; in Andhra, people were addressed by village name with Garu (Uttur Garu). In Maharashtra that became the surname Uttarwar.
av1p2: He grew up on the family farm in Bhamb (Yavatmal district) with childhood memories of school, farm animals, hide-and-seek, and village festivals like Ganesh—where the whole village felt like an extended family. With no local doctor or grocery store, his mother’s home became a kind of pharmacy for first aid. That give-and-take shaped his sense of community.
av2p1: His father pushed for education despite strong opposition from Vijay’s grandfather. There was no school beyond early grades in the village, so Vijay was sent to Nagpur for English-medium schooling—living in a lodge as a seventh-grader with a cousin. Hard years, but formative.
av2p2: He stayed tied to the farm even as a student, helping his father with supervision. He had offers for both engineering and agriculture. His father left the choice to him. Heart won: BSc Agriculture (Akola), then MSc Agronomy (Nagpur)—university topper, gold medalist.
av3p1: In 1983–84, a single computer behind glass in an air-conditioned room at the agriculture university fascinated him. He used Fortran (punch cards) for statistical work instead of manual calculation. US universities admitted him for computer science with prerequisites; he finished coursework in two years plus many extra courses.
av4t: Marriage and a decade in the US
av4p1: Around his green-card interview he needed to marry first. He met Smita, got engaged on 14 January, and married four days later—about 4,000 guests, supported by his doctor father’s goodwill. They went to the US in July 1989, lived there about ten years, then returned to India in 1999. Adjusting back (especially school/society for the family) was hard at first, then settled.
av5p1: Leaving software, he wanted to help farmers. Stevia looked far more profitable than jowar, cotton, or soybean. They launched with a state license—then were told stevia couldn’t be called a sweetener unless officially listed. Rather than shut a ~40-person company, they pivoted to Max Protein. Smita, a self-described foodie, formulated bars in their kitchen (Godrej cupboards of ingredients, food technologist, nutritionist)—~10–15 trials a day for nearly two years until Choco Delight, still selling. Later, farm produce (e.g. mulberry preserves) fed a real farm-to-fork idea at Uttara Farm.
av6t: After Zydus: the wada and return to Bhamb
av6p1: After merging Max Protein with Zydus, they had time to ask “what next?” On a trek near Lonavala they saw a small wada named Rukmai and decided to build something like it in their teak forest in Bhamb—not as a commercial hotel, but a lasting retreat for intellectuals, artists, and rehearsals, meant to stand 100–150 years for children and great-grandchildren. Vijay names nine generations of Uttarwars he wants remembered there, hoping for twelve generations rooted in Bhamb.
av7p1: Yavatmal’s farmer-suicide reputation weighed on him. He couldn’t fix everything, but wanted a “small bit”: raise farmer income so debt and despair ease. He points to prosperous pockets in Maharashtra (Nashik, Pune, Kolhapur, Satara, Bhusawal bananas, western sugar) and asks why not the same model here—high-value crops at scale, with infrastructure.
av7p2: He frames farming like industry: expert growing/hand-holding, supply-chain efficiency, and marketing/distribution. Early work includes ~25 farmers with strong crops; next is scale via cooperative/FPO so “every last rupee goes to the farmer.” Goal: reverse migration—graduates earning ₹25–50k/month living well in the village instead of leaving.
av8p1: Bhamb → Nagpur → US → Mumbai → back to Bhamb—personally and professionally, he describes it as coming full circle: roots, education, tech/business success, then returning to the land and community that made him.
